n: One of the most moving laments in scripture, written during the Babylonian exile (after 587 BC). By Babylon’s rivers and canals the captives sat and wept, remembering Zion.

f.g: The Euphrates and Tigris and their irrigation canals.

n: They hung up their lyres on the poplar trees — too heartbroken to play.
Their captors mockingly demanded entertainment: ‘Sing us one of those Zion songs!’

f.g: Our tormentors, those who plundered us.

n: How can we sing the Lord’s sacred songs in a foreign, pagan land? Holy things shouldn’t be turned into amusement.
The psalmist swears an oath: if I forget Jerusalem, may my right hand — my harp-playing hand — lose its skill.
May my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth — so I could never sing again — if I don’t make Jerusalem my highest joy.
The lament turns to a cry for justice. Edom, Israel’s ‘brother’ nation, cheered as Babylon destroyed Jerusalem: ‘Tear it down to the ground!’

f.g: Raze it — strip it bare, level it.

n: Babylon itself is addressed as ‘daughter’ — a poetic name for a city. The psalmist is confident it will face justice for what it did, as the prophets foretold.

A shocking line of raw grief and rage, echoing the brutal warfare Babylon had inflicted on Jerusalem’s own children. Scripture honestly records this cry for justice; it is a prayer handing vengeance to God, not a command to imitate. Jesus taught us to love and pray for enemies.

f.w: dasheth thy little ones against the stones
